channel.title: Alaska AI Docket
channel.description: Every AI infrastructure decision tracked in Alaska, as it moves. Comment windows, deadlines, votes and filings.

item.title: Air Force land leases for AI data centers at JBER, Eielson and Clear
item.description: A Federal Register search today for Alaska Air Force lease documents published since November 5th returned none, and no award for solicitation AFCEC-26-R-0006 has been announced. Checked and unchanged. The Air Force offered about 4,700 acres across 12 parcels at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Eielson AFB and Clear Space Force Station for privately financed AI data centers. Residents near the five Eielson-area parcels raised noise, permafrost and grid concerns, including one parcel less than a mile from North Pole Middle School. Proposals closed in the spring and are evaluated privately. No public comment period exists and no award timeline has been announced. The solicitation record is public and carries no awardee. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: Enstar's Cook Inlet gas storage plan (Kenai Loop Pool)
item.description: Re-read the Division of Oil and Gas public notice today. Comments on the Kenai Loop storage lease preliminary finding must still be received by 5 p.m. November 13th, and the notice shows no change since October 14th. Checked and unchanged. The Regulatory Commission of Alaska denied Enstar's request for an advance determination that its proposed Cook Inlet gas storage project was prudent, in a 17-page order the Anchorage Daily News reported on July 10th, saying the utility lacked basic information. The $240 million plan would have bought the depleted Kenai Loop Pool from AIX Energy to hold 25 billion cubic feet of gas, close to half Enstar's annual demand, and Enstar suspended it after the order. The commission denied Enstar's petition for reconsideration 3 to 2 on August 21st, with a written order to follow. Enstar applied to the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission on September 17th to store gas in the Kenai Loop field, with a hearing tentatively set for November 12th. On October 13th the Division of Oil and Gas issued a preliminary written finding that a Kenai Loop storage lease to ENSTAR would best serve the state's interest, ahead of Hilcorp's competing application, and public comment on that finding runs until 5 p.m. on November 13th. Anyone may comment on the Division of Oil and Gas's preliminary written finding for the Kenai Loop storage lease until 5 p.m. on November 13th, per the state's public notice. The RCA prudency question stays with the commission, a governor-appointed, legislature-confirmed body whose dockets the public reaches through formal comment and intervention. Status, open-for-comment.

item.title: AIDEA's free state land near Houston, cut to about 6,800 acres
item.description: Decided. DNR posted the signed Final Finding and Decision on its public notice for ADL 234762 today. It reduces the conveyance from 19,500 acres to about 6,800 acres in Township 18 North, Seward Meridian, keeps a reversionary interest, and requires AIDEA to survey the land within 10 years or the decision is void. The parcel was redrawn to avoid the Haessler-Norris trail system, and the remaining 12,700 acres stay under DNR management. Timely commenters may request reconsideration within 20 calendar days. On November 10th Natural Resources Commissioner John Crowther signed the Final Finding and Decision on ADL 234762. It conveys about 6,800 acres of state land about two miles north of Houston to the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority at no cost, down from 19,500 acres in the July 10th preliminary decision, for a multi-use industrial and energy development district. The final decision keeps a reversionary interest that the preliminary decision had waived, and voids the approval if AIDEA does not survey the land and complete the pre-patent requirements within 10 years. DNR received 2,306 public comments and eight from agencies. It says the conveyance does not approve any specific development, and that roads, power and other infrastructure would need their own approvals. The decision is made. People who sent timely written comment may ask the commissioner to reconsider within 20 calendar days of the November 10th decision, which runs to November 30th, with a $200 fee, by mail, fax or dnr.appeals@alaska.gov. If the commissioner does not act within 30 days of the decision the request is considered denied, and a court challenge must start with that request. Anyone else can no longer change the decision at DNR. The lawsuit filed October 22nd in Superior Court at Juneau is still pending, and the next governor is sworn in December 7th. Status, decided.

item.title: Alaska's bid to run its own carbon storage permits
item.description: Re-read EPA's proposed rule, Federal Register document 2026-22085, today. Comments are still due December 14th under docket EPA-HQ-OW-2026-4588, with no correction published. Checked and unchanged. The Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission is applying to the Environmental Protection Agency for primary enforcement authority over Class VI wells, the wells used to inject carbon dioxide for permanent underground storage. If the application succeeds the state, not the federal government, would permit and police every carbon storage well in Alaska. The Environmental Protection Agency is taking written comments on its proposed approval until December 14th, under docket EPA-HQ-OW-2026-4588, and will hold one virtual public hearing during that period. The state's own comment window closed at its May 14th hearing. Status, open-for-comment.

item.title: DeepGreen's underwater data center in Cook Inlet
item.description: The commission's eLibrary record for P-15423, queried today, shows seven filings dated November 6th to 9th, all comments from individuals, six of them filed November 9th in opposition. No order or permit decision is listed. Checked and unchanged. DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV LLC, a Delaware company whose parent formed in January 2026, applied to FERC in February for a preliminary permit over an initial operational envelope of 1,650 acres of Cook Inlet seabed west of Nikiski, proposing a 100 megawatt data center of 66 hives of AI servers powered and cooled by approximately 330 to 350 tidal turbines in water 45 to 166 feet deep. A preliminary permit authorizes study rather than construction, for up to four years, and FERC's Northwest branch found the application incomplete in a June 18th letter. The comment room has closed. Comments, motions to intervene and competing applications on Project No. P-15423-000 were due by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 2nd, 2026, which was 1:00 p.m. Alaska time. FERC now decides whether to grant DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC up to four years of study and site priority. A preliminary permit is not authority to build, and any license application would open a new record. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: The FCC asks whether AI should help run the Universal Service Fund
item.description: A Federal Register search today for documents citing WC Docket No. 26-173 published since October 20th found none about this docket. No order or further notice has been published. Checked and unchanged. The FCC published a notice on August 31st, 2026 seeking comment on how the Universal Service Fund is administered, and nine of its sentences name artificial intelligence. It asks whether AI tools used to review applications, audits and appeal review processes would reduce delays while maintaining accurate results, and whether the fund's administrator should expand use of AI in document review for audits and program compliance. One paragraph poses eight consecutive questions about AI. The Commission is asking rather than proposing, and every AI sentence in the notice is phrased as a question. The same notice seeks comment on cutting the administrator's board from 20 members to 13. Alaska is not named anywhere in it. Alaska's stake is in a companion notice published the same day, WC Docket No. 17-310, which reports that only 34 of 340 approved Telecom Program requests in Alaska in funding year 2025 relied on the Commission's preferred Methods 1 or 2, so the great majority of Alaska's rural health connectivity requests are justified the longer way. That is the paperwork an automated reviewer would read. The comment room has closed. Initial comments closed on September 30th and reply comments on October 30th in WC Docket No. 26-173. The Commission now weighs the record, and an Alaska clinic, school district, library or carrier that did not file reaches the decision only through the delegation or an ex parte meeting under the Commission's rules. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: Fairbanks asks Juneau and Congress to pause data centers
item.description: The Assembly's November 12th agenda, read today, carries no item on Resolution 2026-25 or the moratorium request. The state half still waits for the Legislature to convene on January 19th. Checked and unchanged. On August 27th, 2026 the Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly adopted Resolution 2026-25, its list of 2027 state and federal legislative priorities, sponsored by the Assembly Committee of the Whole. The list carries 25 items, 21 state and 4 federal, and one item appears on both halves. It asks for a moratorium on the permitting, leasing or construction of new commercial data centers on state-owned or municipal lands in Alaska until standards exist for electrical demand, water consumption and shortages, environmental impacts, noise, air quality and land use pollution. Assemblymember Garrett Armstrong moved it onto the state list at an August 6th work session and an amendment replicated it onto the federal list. The request follows the Air Force offer of about 4,700 acres across twelve parcels at three Alaska installations, one of which, Eielson, is inside this borough. The adopted text reaches state and municipal land, not federal land, and KUAC reports Presiding Officer Scott Crass said by phone that federal land was intended too. The borough has already voted, so the room that was open is closed. What the resolution does is hand the question to two bodies that have not acted on it. A reader who wants the moratorium considered asks a legislator to carry it when the Legislature convenes in January 2027, or asks the congressional delegation to take up the federal half. The resolution itself, its full text and the meeting record are public through the borough clerk. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: Fairbanks proposes its own pause on large data center permits
item.description: The Planning Commission's November 10th agenda lists Ordinance No. 2026-42 as item G.4 under public and legislative hearings, after the Regional Comprehensive Plan update. No recommendation or minutes from the hearing were posted tonight. The Assembly's November 12th agenda, read today, does not list the ordinance. Mayor Grier Hopkins's Ordinance No. 2026-42 would accept no land use permit applications for large-scale data centers, and approve no pending ones, through December 31st, 2027. It defines large-scale as 5 MW or more of peak demand, more than 50,000 square feet of data center floor area, or 5 MW or more of onsite generation, and orders a study of energy, air, water and noise within six months. The ordinance goes to the Planning Commission for a recommendation due in 90 days and then back to the elected Assembly, which adopts or rejects it. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: GVEA's $80 million turbine decision
item.description: Re-read Golden Valley's alert page today. It still reports Energy Emergency Alert Level 0, normal operations, as of 7 p.m. on October 24th, with maintenance continuing on a second generation unit and construction underway on the Railbelt Intertie. The page reports no board decision on the turbine purchase. Checked and unchanged. Golden Valley Electric Association is weighing a 60 megawatt naphtha fueled turbine estimated at $80 million, to be installed beside an existing LM6000 at the co-op's North Pole Expansion plant. Its board voted on August 25th, 2026 to keep the purchase alive and to keep studying the risks and the alternatives. A member-owned co-op board decides, in executive session. GVEA members reach it through board elections and member comment periods at regular meetings. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: The Dixon Glacier diversion into Bradley Lake
item.description: Searched the Federal Register today for Alaska documents published November 5th to 9th and found nothing new in Project No. 8221-124 after the October 6th notice. Recommendations remain due November 30th. Checked and unchanged. The Alaska Energy Authority has asked FERC to amend the license for the Bradley Lake Hydroelectric Project, the largest in Alaska, so it can build a new dam diverting meltwater and surface runoff from the Dixon Glacier into Bradley Lake, raise the lake's normal maximum operating pool by about 16 feet, and install a 0.3 megawatt micro-hydro turbine in one of the dam's fishwater release valves. The application projects about 38 percent more average annual generation while installed capacity rises from 119.7 to 120.0 megawatts, because the gain comes from water rather than from turbines. AEA estimates construction at about $400 million and about three years of study and permitting followed by three years of construction. FERC accepting the application for filing is a procedural step and not an approval. The comment window has closed. Anyone could file a comment, a motion to intervene or a protest in docket P-8221-124 until 5:00 p.m. Eastern on August 28th, 2026, which was 1:00 p.m. Alaska time, and that hour has passed. FERC now weighs the application and has published no decision date. The docket itself stays readable through FERC's eLibrary, so an Alaskan can follow what was filed without being able to add to it. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: The Air Force nuclear microreactor at Eielson
item.description: Searched the Federal Register today for Alaska documents published November 5th to 9th and found no Air Force, Oklo or reactor notice. The base's microreactor page refused an automated read today. Checked and unchanged. The Air Force intends to award Oklo a 30 year fixed price power purchase agreement for a microreactor delivering up to 5 megawatts to Eielson Air Force Base outside Fairbanks. Oklo would build, own and operate it, and the contract is signed only after Oklo obtains a license from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The comment window on the Air Force's preferred site near Spruce Lake closed on September 30th, and no extension was announced. The Air Force now weighs what it received and has published no date for a decision. The contract itself follows a Nuclear Regulatory Commission license. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: An 89 million dollar federal grant for a coal plant in the Susitna watershed
item.description: Re-read the Department of Energy's project selections page today. It still lists Terra Energy Center Corporation of Anchorage for engineering and design of a 1,250 MW coal plant with carbon capture in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, and reports no signed award and no cancellation. Checked and unchanged. The Department of Energy selected Terra Energy Center Corporation of Anchorage, an affiliate of Flatlands Energy, for an 89 million dollar grant to study a 1,250 megawatt coal fired power plant west of Skwentna, with a 60 mile pipeline carrying its carbon dioxide to Beluga for injection into a depleted gas reservoir. The money funds a viability assessment rather than construction, and Terra must match it. The grant selection carried no public comment period. Comment rooms open later, when the mine, the plant, the pipeline and the injection well each need their own permits. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: The federal bill that would make a 100 megawatt customer pay for its own wires
item.description: The bill status record GovInfo publishes, read today and last updated October 31st, still ends on September 30th, when the motion to proceed was withdrawn in the Senate. The Senate's lame-duck session opens today and no new action is recorded. Checked and unchanged. H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, would add a standard to the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act requiring that rates charged a large-load customer recover from that customer the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission or distribution upgrade needed to serve it, and keep recovering it if the customer walks away. A large-load customer is a non-residential consumer with aggregate peak demand of 100 megawatts or more at one site or campus, running information technology infrastructure for data storage and computation, which is a data center described without the phrase. State regulators would get one year from enactment to begin considering it and two to decide. A state is excused if, before enactment, it implemented a comparable standard, conducted a proceeding on one, or its legislature voted on one. Alaska's Senate passed SB 250, a comparable cost-allocation bill, on May 16th, and the House never voted. Whether one chamber satisfies the words the State legislature has voted is unresolved, and it decides whether Alaska is already excused. There is no comment room on a bill. The route is the congressional delegation, and after enactment it becomes a proceeding at the Regulatory Commission of Alaska, which is a room with a docket and a public record. The House passed the bill on September 16th and the Senate declined to take it up on September 30th, so it waits on the lame-duck session that opens November 9th. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: Renting the highway shoulder to power and fiber, with data centers named as the draw
item.description: Searched the Federal Register today for Alaska documents published November 5th to 9th and found no Department of Transportation corridors notice. Written comments closed October 2nd and the department has not said when it will act. Checked and unchanged. A request for information launching America's Great Corridors of Commerce, a voluntary program letting highway and rail right-of-way owners raise revenue by colocating utility infrastructure in their corridors through public-private partnerships. Transmission, fiber, rural broadband and water pipelines are all named. One stated aim is to incentivize data centers, manufacturing facilities and distribution hubs to locate close to the corridors. Alaska has four long corridors and a railroad, and every large compute proposal in the state is shaped around one of them, yet the notice does not mention Alaska and frames the program around multi-state corridors, a shape no Alaskan right-of-way has. The written comment period under docket DOT-OST-2026-3269 closed on October 2nd. The notice says late comments will be considered to the extent practicable, so a filing at regulations.gov is still possible, though a reading is no longer assured. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: A second power line between Southcentral and the Interior, Beluga to Healy
item.description: Re-read the Department of Energy's October 5th release today. It still describes up to $150 million in Defense Production Act funding combined with $268 million in non-federal funding for about 223 miles of new line, a planned $418 million in all, and reports no signed agreement. Checked and unchanged. On October 5th the Department of Energy announced its intent to put up to $150 million of Defense Production Act funding into the Alaska Energy Authority's Beluga-Healy Transmission Project, a second high-voltage connection between Southcentral and Interior Alaska. DOE counts on $268 million in non-federal funding for a preliminary estimate of about $418 million, and about 223 miles of new line. The Railbelt now relies on a single corridor, AEA's 170-mile Alaska Intertie between Willow and Healy, built in the mid-1980s. Energy Secretary Chris Wright tied the award to the military expansion under way in Alaska and to mining. The release does not mention data centers, though the Air Force has offered about 4,700 acres at JBER, Eielson and Clear for them. The Energy Department chose this project under the Defense Production Act, and none of the announcements names a public comment period or a hearing. The Alaska Energy Authority, which proposed the line, now has to find the rest of the money. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: Alaska's second year of rural health transformation money
item.description: Tracked. Read the CMS award table and the state's final Year 1 award list today. CMS announced Year 2 Rural Health Transformation awards on November 9th, and Alaska's $272,653,149 is second only to Texas. Year 1 closed October 22nd with just under $249 million to 254 projects, seven of which buy an AI tool. Fall applications closed October 28th. Alaskans reach the next round through an applying clinic, tribe, city or nonprofit. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: STAK Energy's North Slope AI campus lease
item.description: Re-read the DNR notice for ADL 422741 today. It still carries the May 12th preliminary decision and its attachments, last modified June 17th, and no final finding and decision is posted. Checked and unchanged. A preliminary decision would give STAK Energy a 50-year lease on 715.4 acres of state land about 26 miles south of Deadhorse for a gas-fired AI and cloud campus its developer pegs at more than $10 billion, with 1 to 3 gigawatts of on-site generation. More than 500 public comments arrived before the first deadline; fewer than a dozen supported the project. The written comment window closed 4:30 p.m. July 17th, 2026. DNR now weighs more than 500 comments before a final best-interest decision on the 50-year lease. No public comment path remains open. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: The AI ratepayer pledge, and which Alaska utilities have signed it
item.description: Re-read the White House signatory list today. It still counts 327 signatories, 207 cooperatives, 72 utilities and 48 data center developers, the same as on November 4th. Checked and unchanged. The White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge asks AI companies, utilities and data center developers to commit that new data center load pays for its own generation and delivery instead of shifting the cost onto households. USA TODAY and POWER both describe it as voluntary and non binding. Gov. Mike Dunleavy signed the governors addendum on July 23rd, 2026, one of 23 governors. The signatory list has grown from 281 when it was first read here on July 26th, 2026 to 324 on October 10th, and across that growth exactly one Alaska entity appears on it, Cordova Electric Cooperative, a 1,566 customer cooperative that is not connected by transmission line to any other community. No Railbelt utility has signed. Alaska's electric cooperatives are governed by boards their own members elect, so a member can ask their board directly whether it intends to sign. A voluntary federal pledge has no public comment docket, which is why this room is indirect rather than open. Status, watching.

item.title: Alaska's statewide speech-to-text contract
item.description: Re-read the state's public notice for RFP 2026-0200-0064 today. It still shows Amendment 1 and the August 28th proposal deadline, last modified August 17th, with no notice of intent to award. Checked and unchanged. Alaska is soliciting one statewide contract to convert speech, live or recorded, into written text for general, medical and legal records. The notice says every state governmental entity may use the resulting contract, naming the Legislative Branch, the Court System, the University of Alaska, boards and commissions, cities, boroughs, school districts and federally recognized tribes. The public notice does not use the terms artificial intelligence, machine learning or automated speech recognition. A vendor solicitation, not a rulemaking, so no public comment period exists. Proposals closed August 28th and are evaluated privately. The notice and the named procurement officer are public, though the notice's own archive date has now passed. No award has been posted. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: DMV asks vendors about automated compliance for commercial licenses
item.description: Re-read the state's public notice for RFI 02-101-27 today. It still shows Amendment One, last modified August 7th, and names no follow-on solicitation. Checked and unchanged. The Division of Motor Vehicles asked vendors for products, services, technical approaches and industry best practices related to automated compliance and data integration systems supporting the commercial driver's license program. The public notice does not use the terms artificial intelligence or machine learning. A request for information gathers vendor input before any solicitation. There is no public comment path and no decision is made at this stage. Status, watching.

item.title: A national AI institute for Native communities, and the Alaska lane that closed with it
item.description: Re-read the Grants.gov listing today. It is still archived as of September 26th, with one award of $2.5 million to $3.5 million expected and no recipient named. Checked and unchanged. The Administration for Native Americans published its final Fiscal Year 2026 program policies on July 28th, 2026, standing up three funding opportunities and leaving out SEDS-AK, the Alaska-specific economic development program that ran alongside SEDS for decades. Two days later it posted the AI3 Action Institute, a single national award of up to $3,500,000 to build an artificial intelligence resource center for Native communities, with Alaska Native villages under ANCSA and nonprofit village consortia named as eligible applicants. Only eligible applicants reached this one, and applications closed on August 27th, 2026, so no public path remains. An Alaskan reached it through a tribe, an ANCSA village or a Native nonprofit that filed in time. Applications are evaluated privately and no awardee has been named. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: The executive order that lets big data centers skip the usual federal review
item.description: Searched the Federal Register today for documents citing Executive Order 14318 published since November 1st and found none. Checked and unchanged. Executive Order 14318, Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure, directs federal agencies to speed approvals for data centers adding more than 100 megawatts of load or costing at least 500 million dollars. It tells agencies to find and create categorical exclusions under the National Environmental Policy Act, and directs Interior and Energy to offer federal sites while Defense may competitively lease military land. An executive order takes no public comment. Its effect is to remove review steps that would otherwise have carried one, so the room this closes is the environmental review a project would have had. Status, watching.

item.title: The University of Alaska's 829 acres at Port MacKenzie, leased to the coal plant's campus
item.description: A news search today found nothing newer than the Alaska Journal of Commerce's October 26th republication of the October 6th report on the lease. Checked and unchanged. Terra Energy signed a 20 year lease with the University of Alaska in late May for 829 acres near Port MacKenzie, four parcels in Township 14 North, Range 4 West, Seward Meridian, for what the lease calls the Terra Energy Center Campus, a large-scale industrial park. The project is part of affiliate Flatlands Energy's plan for a coal plant near Skwentna, which the Department of Energy selected for $89 million in engineering funding and whose described loads include data centers. Rent is $20,000 in the first year, $60,000 a year in the second and third, and $586,000 a year once operations begin, targeted for 2030, with a 2 percent annual adjustment. Borough officials expect Terra to pursue about 1,000 acres of borough port land as well. The university's notice of intent to lease took written comments from January 30th to March 2nd and named no tenant and no use. University land is exempt from the state's best interest finding, according to the Mat-Su Sentinel. The next public room is the Mat-Su Borough Assembly, if Terra asks to lease borough land at the port. Status, decided.

item.title: The Kenai Peninsula school district's AI rulebook
item.description: The district's agenda site returned a server error again today and could not be re-read. BP 5131.9 and AR 5131.9 stand as last published. The Kenai Peninsula Borough School District is writing the rules for artificial intelligence in its 39 schools while the school year starts. Its Policy Review Committee took up AR 5131.9 Academic Honesty, a new administrative regulation the district says was brought forward in relation to the inclusion of AI, on August 3rd, 2026, with two competing drafts posted, one from Administration and one from board member Mica VanBuskirk. That same evening the full board took first readings on three more documents the district describes as revised for AI-related policy shifts, AR 5125 Student Records, BP 1114 Communication Using Electronic Media and BP 5131.9 Academic Honesty, plus AR 6161.4 Acceptable Use. The board adopted both academic honesty documents on September 14th, BP 5131.9 on a second reading and AR 5131.9 as a new administrative regulation, inside a single unanimous consent agenda motion. The rest of the package has no adoption recorded. The district told KBBI in July that it has spent 8,300 dollars to date on a three year MagicSchool subscription for students and staff, so the classroom AI tool was bought before the rulebook was finished. Upstream sits Alaska's Strategic Framework, Artificial Intelligence for K-12, issued by the Department of Education and Early Development, which means what Kenai adopts previews what other Alaska districts face. An elected school board decides, and its regular meetings carry a public comment period. There is no formal comment window on these documents and no published date for a final vote, so an Alaskan reaches this one through a board member or from the podium at a meeting. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: Which grid equipment gets restricted, and the reason given is AI
item.description: Searched the Federal Register today for Energy Department documents on the bulk-power system published since November 1st. Two FERC notices turned up and neither follows up this request for information. Checked and unchanged. A request for information implementing the August 26th emergency declaration on securing the United States bulk-power system. It asks which equipment and transactions should count as covered, naming grid-connected inverters, battery energy storage, universal power systems, generators and industrial control systems. The notice grounds the emergency in a finding that rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, data centers, artificial intelligence and defense production has increased the nation's dependence on abundant, reliable electricity. Alaska's Railbelt and rural utilities are mid-buildout on the inverter and storage categories listed, so a restriction reprices projects already in planning. The written response period under docket DOE-HQ-2026-1123 closed on October 9th. The department has not said when it will act on the responses. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: The University of Alaska's AI policy
item.description: The regents' board pages returned server errors again today, and no published report of the outcome of the scheduled November 5th vote on AI Engaged was found. On November 5th five faculty members, among them James Ryan, chair of the UA Statewide Advisory Committee, answered the November 4th opinion piece in the Anchorage Daily News. They wrote that AI use in the original draft was not concealed, that adding a small AI attribution was a good move, and that they would prefer the statement take a more neutral stance toward AI. A mandatory University of Alaska security standard has governed generative AI use across the system since January 2025, while the university's own guidance page, last updated March 11th, 2025, still says UA System regulations are currently under development. University leadership plans to submit a finalized draft artificial intelligence policy for approval at the November regents meeting, which KTOO reports would require all three campuses to develop AI plans for their communities. There is no comment room on this one yet. The university says it plans listening sessions and online surveys this fall, and as of September 16th no session dates had been scheduled. The document binding users today is a security standard issued through the Office of Information Technology rather than anything the regents have voted on, and it has been in effect since January 2025. It applies to the UA System and all users of UA computing resources, and violations may subject employees to disciplinary action up to and including termination and students to disciplinary action including expulsion. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: Petersburg drafts a nine-month data center pause
item.description: KFSK's coverage, read today, has nothing newer than its November 2nd preview of the first reading. No vote and no second reading date have been reported. Checked and unchanged. On September 21st the Petersburg Borough Assembly tied 3 to 3 on starting the year-long data center moratorium the Planning Commission had asked for. On October 5th it voted unanimously to start two measures instead. Vice Mayor Jeigh Stanton Gregor's would have staff draft an ordinance pausing building permits for nine months for data centers that rely on on-site power generation or lack closed-loop cooling, while projects connecting to Petersburg's grid could still apply. Assembly Member Jeff Meucci's directs the borough manager to prepare amendments to the Title 19 zoning code to regulate data centers. Stanton Gregor's proposal aims to cover the whole borough except Kupreanof, where the earlier request covered only the municipal service area. In September, Utility Director Steve Harbour said selling that much power to one customer could significantly blunt how much electric rates will increase, and KFSK reported the borough utility has endorsed a small data center proposed by Mazzella Alaska LLC, with no megawatt figure given. The Assembly has directed staff to draft the moratorium and zoning ordinances. KFSK reports both must return to the Assembly for consideration and public hearings before either can take effect, so residents can testify then. No hearing date has been set. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: North Slope Power, the borough's gas plant for AI data centers
item.description: A news search today found nothing newer than The Alaska Current's October 3rd report on the borough's plant. Checked and unchanged. The North Slope Borough and Twenty First Century Utilities are developing North Slope Power, a gas-fired plant near Prudhoe Bay planned at 3 gigawatts in its first phase and meant to scale to 10, to deliver electricity to colocated AI data centers. As reported by the Alaska Current, the borough has funded a $1.2 million no-bid feasibility contract and committed another $5 million in public funds. The borough commits money to North Slope Power by Assembly resolution and mayoral contract, so the elected borough government is the path in. The deal's financial structure has not been made public. Status, watching.

item.title: AIDEA's $75 million fiber investment subsidiary
item.description: AIDEA's meeting schedule, read today, shows the November 4th board meeting continued to November 6th, with Amended Resolution G25-07 on the Ambler Access Project added. Neither day lists an item on Northstar Fiber Development or Resolution G26-11, and minutes for both are not yet posted. The next regular meeting is December 4th. AIDEA's board adopted Resolution G26-11 forming Northstar Fiber Development LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary that may invest up to $75 million in subsea and terrestrial fiber, landing stations and middle-mile networks, with Pacific connectivity first. The resolution picks no project, route or partner, and the executive director's power to commit funds under it expires December 31st, 2028. The board adopted the resolution on October 21st. Any project the executive director approves under it is reported to the board at its next meeting, and the board's public meetings are the place to be heard. The next are listed for November 4th and December 4th. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: AEA shops for the cable under Cook Inlet
item.description: AEA's project page, read today, still lists the link as in development at an estimated $413 million, with $142.5 million still required and completion targeted for 2032. Responses to the cable request remain due December 15th. Checked and unchanged. The Alaska Energy Authority is asking submarine cable makers and installers to prequalify for the Cook Inlet PowerLink, a direct current link between Beluga and Nikiski that AEA says would remove the single point of failure between the Kenai Peninsula and Anchorage. The base bid is a 100 MW cable, procurement is expected about June 2027 and service in December 2031. AEA lists $142.5 million of a $413 million cost as still required. DeepGreen, an AI data center applicant at FERC, named the line its strategic partner and later said it holds no agreement with AEA. A vendor solicitation, not a rulemaking, so no public comment period exists. Responses are due 2:00 p.m. Alaska time December 15th. The public reaches the decision through AEA's board meetings and the project's later environmental review, expected to finish in early 2029. Status, pending-decision.

item.title: Copper Valley Electric's shelved nuclear reactor study
item.description: Re-read the cooperative's project page today. Its newest item is still the August 9th, 2023 release headed that the micro modular reactor project was tabled indefinitely, and nothing dated 2024 or later has been added. Checked and unchanged. Copper Valley Electric studied putting a 10 megawatt micro modular reactor into its isolated Glennallen and Valdez system, which is connected to no other utility and burns liquid fossil fuel for roughly a third of its power. The cooperative finished a pre feasibility study, published it, and then tabled the project indefinitely. Copper Valley Electric is a member owned cooperative, so its board answers to ratepayers who elect it. The project is tabled, so there is nothing before the board to comment on now. Status, closed.

item.title: Anchorage's surveillance rules for its police crime center
item.description: The Assembly passed the administration-backed substitute, AO 2026-108(S) as amended, 11 to 1 late on Wednesday night, November 4th, according to Alaska's News Source, which did not name the member voting no. An amendment by Vice Chair Daniel Volland and Sydney Scout to write a 14-day deletion deadline for plate reader captures and crime center video into municipal code failed, and an amendment requiring judicial warrants for retrospective plate reader searches failed 5 to 7. An amendment by Erin Baldwin Day, passed unanimously, requires 30 days of advance notice to the Assembly before APD makes a material policy change, and a change to data storage limits counts as one. APD's own policy already deletes plate data after 14 days. The same night the Assembly voted 10 to 1 to create a temporary committee, led by Kameron Perez-Verdia, to oversee APD policies, meeting at least monthly for one year (Anchorage Daily News). The as-amended text was not readable on the municipality's site today, which returned not found for every AO 2026-108 document. Three Anchorage Assembly members, Keith McCormick, Sydney Scout and Vice Chair Daniel Volland, introduced an ordinance on August 18th, reported as AO-2026-108, that would write surveillance rules into Anchorage code, among them a case number for every search of surveillance data, deletion of individuals' data after two weeks unless it is evidence in an active investigation, a warrant before footage goes to out of state or federal agencies, limits on automatic license plate readers, and, in co-sponsor Scout's own words, Assembly approval before adding new surveillance capabilities including AI powered tracking or identification technology. It moves alongside a roughly $600,000 contract with ThunderCat Technology for equipment at the Real Time Crime Center, the system the Assembly funded with $11.8 million last year and which is designed to stream up to 750 camera feeds. The center opened in September 2025 with one employee and about 15 cameras. The Assembly passed the ordinance on November 4th, so the vote is over. The new temporary oversight committee will meet publicly at least once a month for a year, which is the next public room where these rules get reviewed, and an Assembly member is the route to any change. Status, decided.

item.title: The Army's Janus microreactor program at Fort Wainwright
item.description: Re-read the DefenseScoop report today. The five Janus installations named on August 26th are Fort Bragg, Fort Campbell, Fort Hood, Fort Benning and Fort Drum, and Fort Wainwright is among the short-listed sites not chosen. Checked and unchanged. Fort Wainwright was one of nine Army posts short listed for a microreactor under the Janus program. On August 26th, 2026 the Army named the first five installations and their vendors, and Fort Wainwright was not among them. Industry submissions were taken through the Defense Innovation Unit and are evaluated privately. No public comment period exists at this stage, and no vendor has been named for Fort Wainwright. Status, decided.

item.title: FCC lets GCI buy Quintillion's Arctic subsea fiber
item.description: Added. Read today against the FCC's order DA 26-1124, released October 20th, including its conditions in Appendix A. Broadband Breakfast reported GCI's statement on October 26th that the approval is an important step to completing the transaction, which has not yet closed. On October 20th the FCC approved, with conditions, the transfer of control of Quintillion's submarine cable landing license to GCI and denied Alaska Communications' petition to deny. The 1,176-mile Quintillion System connects Prudhoe Bay, Utqiagvik, Wainwright, Point Hope, Kotzebue and Nome, and its Nome to Homer Express extension adds landings at Emmonak, Hooper Bay and Naknek. Alaska Communications argued that GCI and Quintillion are the only middle mile providers for substantial portions of Western and Northern Alaska. The FCC found the concerns largely mitigated, citing the growing presence of low Earth orbit satellite providers, particularly Starlink, while acknowledging disagreement in the record over whether Starlink sells wholesale middle mile service in Alaska today. As conditions, GCI must honor Quintillion's existing contracts and pricing for the life of the system, may adjust prices for inflation only when Anchorage inflation tops 5 percent and no sooner than three years after closing, and must file larger contracts with the FCC for five to seven years. The deal carries a $310 million enterprise value. The order does not mention artificial intelligence or data centers. The order is decided. Petitions for reconsideration or applications for review may be filed within thirty days of its October 20th release, under the FCC's own rules. GCI must give the FCC its larger wholesale and enterprise contracts on the Quintillion network under seal, so the prices stay out of public view. Status, decided.

item.title: HB 259, state utility standards for large data centers
item.description: The morning sweep of the Legislature's BASIS record still reports HB 259 in House Energy with a status date of January 20th. The bill died in committee at sine die on May 20th. Checked and unchanged. HB 259, introduced by Rep. Donna Mears in January 2026, would have set utility rate-setting guidelines and community benefit agreement standards for large energy use facilities such as data centers, and given the Regulatory Commission of Alaska new duties over them. The House Energy Committee heard it twice, on January 29th and February 3rd, 2026, taking testimony from Greensparc, GCI, the Alaska Municipal League and former Rep. Paul Seaton. It never advanced out of that committee, and it carried a second referral to House Community and Regional Affairs it never reached. The bill died with the 34th Legislature at sine die on May 20th, 2026. Alaska still has no statewide cost-allocation rule governing how a large data-center load is billed against other ratepayers, which leaves that question with the Regulatory Commission of Alaska and with individual utility boards. The bill died when the Legislature adjourned. No public path remains to this vehicle. A constituent who wants these standards has to ask a legislator to introduce them again in the 35th Legislature, which convenes in January 2027. Status, closed.

item.title: SB 250, who pays for a data center's power
item.description: The morning sweep of the Legislature's BASIS record still reports SB 250 in House Community and Regional Affairs with a status date of May 17th and no later action. Checked and unchanged. SB 250, introduced by Sen. Loki Tobin on February 18th, would have barred utilities from putting a data center's costs into anyone's rates unless those costs were recovered solely from the data center, and would have required the Regulatory Commission of Alaska to approve each data center contract. The Senate-passed version applied to data centers drawing 15 megawatts of peak demand from an electric utility. The Senate passed it 14 to 5 on May 16th, and the House Community and Regional Affairs Committee heard and held it on May 18th, its last recorded action. The bill stalled in a House committee before the session ended. Any revival starts over in the next Legislature, where it goes to the legislators you elect on November 3rd. Status, closed.

item.title: AIDEA's $25 million stake in microreactor maker NuCube
item.description: Read AIDEA's release and NuCube's SEC filing. The $25 million counts toward the $75 million minimum cash condition for NuCube's merger with Launch Two Acquisition Corp. AIDEA says project costs and energy savings will be determined as projects are developed. AIDEA agreed to buy $25 million of NuCube Energy's Class A shares at $9.25 each, which NuCube's filing calls about a 14.5 percent discount, with half a warrant per share at $11.50. AIDEA's release names data centers among the industries cheaper power could serve and names no Alaska site, utility, customer or date. AIDEA announced the investment as made on October 21st. The company's merger filing describes AIDEA as its anchor investor. No public comment step was announced. Status, decided.

item.title: The AKLNG gas line tax bill
item.description: Checked for news of the tax bill today. Nothing has moved since the third special session ended on August 25th; the next vehicle remains the Legislature seated in January under the governor elected November 3rd. A conference committee compromise unveiled July 2nd would swap the state property tax on the Glenfarne-led Alaska LNG project for a volumetric tax after five years of operation or 500 MMcf per day, and extend the completion deadline to the end of 2034. The House deadlocked 19 to 19 on July 16th over an expanded S corporation income tax, the governor rejected that provision, and a third special session convened July 27th with no bill from the governor and almost no legislators in the room. Legislators decide; constituents reach them directly. The gas line would feed the grid most Alaska compute would ride on. Status, closed.

item.title: Mat-Su bans automated license plate readers
item.description: Checked the borough's legislative record again today. Ordinance Serial No. 26-106 still shows as passed on September 15th, with no later action. Checked and unchanged. Ordinance Serial No. 26-106 adopts a new borough code chapter, MSB 23.30, whose title states that it prohibits the acquisition, installation and operation of automated license plate reader systems and associated mass surveillance technology. Assemblymember Bernier moved to introduce it on September 1st and to set the public hearing. A motion to adopt carried on September 15th. The borough's legislative record contradicts itself on who moved adoption, its action text naming one member and its structured mover field another, so this record does not name that mover. It is a prohibition rather than a set of conditions, which makes it the opposite instrument to the surveillance rules the neighbouring Anchorage Assembly is weighing. The borough's legislative record carries no vote tally for either motion, only that each one passed. The Assembly adopted the ordinance on September 15th, so there is no comment room left on this measure. The borough code it creates, MSB 23.30, is the public record of what was decided, and an Assembly member is the route to any change to it. Status, decided.

item.title: The Navy's permit for an under-ice robot navigation grid
item.description: Searched the Federal Register today for Office of Naval Research Arctic documents published since September 11th and found none, so the authorization published September 10th stands with no correction or withdrawal. Checked and unchanged. NMFS has authorized the Office of Naval Research to harass marine mammals incidental to Year 9 of its Arctic Research Activities in the Beaufort and Chukchi seas, and what the authorization covers is an acoustic navigation grid. Up to six moored sources at 900 to 950 Hz and two drifting ice gateway buoys will transmit a 30 second pulse every four hours for one year, so that gliders operating under sea ice can fix a position by trilateration from those sources rather than by dead reckoning. The study area is about 639,237 square kilometres across the US Exclusive Economic Zone, the high seas north of Alaska and part of the Canadian Exclusive Economic Zone, coming within 204 kilometres of the Alaska coast at its nearest point. A research cruise of 22 days is planned to begin September 22nd, 2026 aboard R/V Sikuliaq, US Coast Guard Cutter HEALY or another vessel, while the sound sources stay in the water for twelve months. The authorization covers Level B harassment only and states that take by Level A harassment is neither anticipated nor authorized. The record on this one is shut. NMFS took comment for 30 days after publishing the proposed authorization on July 22nd, 2026 and received three comment letters, all from private citizens, then issued the authorization on September 10th, 2026. There is no open filing path now. The next door is the Year 10 renewal, which the Year 9 proposal already invited comment on inside its own action line, and no renewal notice has published. Anyone who wants standing in Year 10 should watch the Federal Register for a proposed authorization under docket RTID 0648-XF889 or its successor. Status, decided.

item.title: Kenai Peninsula Borough writes a weather modification code
item.description: Enacted. The borough's legislative record shows two Assembly actions on October 20th, a motion by Niesen to amend the ordinance and a motion by Truesdell to enact it as amended, and both carried. KDLL reported that the amendments added a requirement to describe the intended outcome of the activity and a ban on geoengineering on borough land designated for casual use, and that the new section of code is effective immediately. Mayor Peter Micciche told KDLL the borough's ability to limit weather modification and geoengineering is limited to borough lands, and Alaska DNR has said state law does not address the activity. Ordinance 2026-35, sponsored by the mayor, would amend borough code to enact a new section, KPB 17.10.165, related to weather modification and geoengineering activities on borough lands. It was introduced on September 3rd, carried a September 15th agenda date in the Policies and Procedures Committee, and is set for public hearing on October 20th. A companion measure, Resolution 2026-046, is on the same agenda. The borough took up the subject after a California company flew drone based cloud seeding over the Kenai Peninsula in August. The ordinance would require ten items in a borough lease or land use permit application, prohibit the activity on borough lands open for casual use, and carry a $1,000 per day fine and a five year application ban for a missing closeout summary. Its reach is borough land; the August flight that prompted it was over state land. The borough's record now carries an October 6th agenda date in the Policies and Procedures Committee. The Assembly enacted the ordinance as amended on October 20th, after its public hearing, and the new code section is in effect. It reaches borough land only. Status, decided.

item.title: Anchorage data-center zoning ordinance AO 2026-27
item.description: Re-read the text of AO 2026-27 on the Assembly's site today. It still defines data centers and similar energy-intensive facilities for land use review, as adopted on March 27th. Checked and unchanged. On March 27th, 2026 the Anchorage Assembly adopted ordinance AO 2026-27 in a 10 to 2 vote, defining data centers in the municipal zoning code for the first time. It confines them to commercial and industrial zones, requires landscaping buffers and enclosed power equipment, and requires written statements from electric and water utilities that the grid has sufficient system capacity before a project proceeds. Members Scott Myers and Keith McCormick voted against it. The elected Anchorage Assembly adopted the ordinance in a public 10 to 2 vote. Residents reach it through Assembly elections and public testimony. Status, decided.
